overview: Security governance is how an organization directs and checks its security work: who decides, which rules apply, how risk is handled and how anyone knows it is working. This domain covers four connected ideas: planning governance, risk and compliance (GRC); keeping the business running through redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery; building security awareness; and measuring whether security is effective. Each idea now includes how artificial intelligence (AI) changes the picture.
analogy: Think of running a community hospital. The board sets direction and answers for results, department heads own their areas, and staff follow written procedures and the law. Backup generators and a second supply route keep care going when the power fails or a road floods, and regular drills prove the plans work. Every new hire learns to question a stranger asking for patient records. Each month, leaders read a short report on infection rates, wait times and early warnings. Security governance works the same way for information.

topics.overview: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) joins three jobs that often sit apart: setting direction, managing risk and meeting obligations. Planning GRC well means everyone knows who is accountable, which rules apply and how the organization proves it follows them. This topic covers why GRC matters, how to plan it, accountability, frameworks, tools and the risk register, and how to govern the use of AI.
can_do: Explain what each part of GRC does and why joining them closes gaps and cuts duplicated work
Use a RACI chart so every GRC task has exactly one accountable person
Tell a legal or contract obligation from a voluntary framework, and map one set of controls to several frameworks
Use risk tolerances, the risk register and an AI acceptable use policy in everyday GRC work

subtopics.name: GRC Purpose and Importance
subtopics.definition: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) is a coordinated way to direct an organization, manage its risks and meet its obligations, using shared owners and records.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Run as separate silos, the three duplicate work, miss gaps and give leaders conflicting pictures. GRC gives one shared view of risk that serves business goals.
how_it_works: Governance sets direction: leaders set goals, assign accountability and oversee results.
Risk management finds, rates and treats risks to those goals, within limits leaders set.
Compliance confirms obligations are met and keeps the evidence to prove it.
All three share one set of records, so one control can meet several needs.

rows.label: Main question
cells: Who decides, and where are we going?
What could stop us, and what do we do about it?
Are we meeting our obligations, and can we prove it?

rows.label: Led by
cells: Risk owners, supported by security and risk teams
The compliance function, with control owners

subtopics.example: A logistics firm keeps its privacy checklist in legal, its risk list in IT and its policies in human resources. One backup control is tested three times, while a contract's breach-notice clause has no owner. Leadership creates one GRC program, and Omar, a junior analyst, maps each obligation to a control, exposing the unowned clause as a gap.

review: Record the agreed owner on each policy, risk or obligation entry you add
Link each new obligation to the risks and controls it affects
evidence: Shared control library mapped to risks and obligations
Compliance calendar of reporting deadlines
audit_focus.recommend: Raise mismatches between risk records and obligations with the GRC program owner.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management sets GRC direction and approves the program

subtopics.isaca_rule: GRC exists so security serves business goals. Its value is alignment, clear accountability and one shared view of risk, not any single tool. Practitioners keep records accurate and flag gaps.

exam_traps.trap: GRC is a software product the security team buys and runs.
exam_traps.why: Tools support GRC, but GRC is a management approach. A platform without owners and decisions changes nothing.

exam_traps.trap: Being compliant means the organization is secure.
exam_traps.why: Compliance shows certain obligations were met at a point in time. Risks outside those rules, and new threats, remain.

key_terms.definition: One list of the organization's controls, each with an owner, mapped to the risks and obligations it covers.
Making sure security work supports business goals instead of competing with them.

subtopics.name: Planning a GRC Program
subtopics.definition: Planning a governance, risk and compliance (GRC) program means setting its scope, owners and obligations first, so effort goes where risk is greatest.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a plan, a program copies someone else's checklist and protects the wrong things. A plan gives leaders something to approve, fund and measure.
how_it_works: Understand the mission, the critical services and how much risk leaders will take.
List the obligations that apply, from laws and contracts to internal policies.
Set the scope, meaning which units, systems and data are covered, and choose a framework.
Give each policy, risk and control an owner, and have senior management approve a charter and budget.
subtopics.example: A small online bookseller starts taking card payments and selling abroad. Before buying tools, the owner has the IT lead list what now applies: card industry rules, privacy law and the payment provider's contract. Ines, a new support technician, inventories the in-scope staff laptops so the plan starts from an accurate list.

review: Check the systems and data you support against the program scope
Note sensitive data handled outside the scope
evidence: Signed program charter with budget and scope
Obligations list with an owner for each duty
audit_focus.recommend: Send any system or data set missing from the scope to the program owner.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management signs off the program before work begins

subtopics.isaca_rule: Plan before you buy. Understand the business and its obligations first, then set scope, owners and a framework, and only then choose tools.

exam_traps.trap: Start a GRC program by buying a platform or running a vulnerability scan.
exam_traps.why: Without known obligations, scope and owners, a tool has nothing to measure against and scan results have no priority.

exam_traps.trap: Copy a large company's policy set to save time.
exam_traps.why: Obligations and risks differ by organization. Borrowed policies can miss required duties or demand controls nobody can run.

key_terms.definition: A short approved document stating a program's purpose, authority, scope and sponsor.
A duty set by law, regulation, contract or the organization's own policy.

subtopics.name: GRC Accountability: RACI and Reporting Lines
subtopics.definition: Accountability in governance, risk and compliance (GRC) means every task, risk and control has one named person who answers for it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When everyone is involved but no one is accountable, decisions stall and gaps go unowned.
how_it_works: The governance roles themselves are taught in 1.3.1; here they are assigned to GRC work.
A RACI chart (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) maps each task to people; the table below explains each letter.
Each task has exactly one Accountable person; several can be Responsible.
Senior management approves policy, funds the program and decides on risk above tolerance; risk owners accept risk within it.
Reporting lines carry risk and compliance results upward, often through a risk committee to the board.

rows.label: Meaning
cells: Answers for the result and signs it off
Gives input before the work is done

rows.label: Example: quarterly access review
cells: The IT administrator who pulls the access lists
Department managers, who confirm who needs access
The security team and the risk committee

subtopics.example: A furniture maker's yearly supplier security review was skipped: procurement thought IT did it, and IT thought procurement did. The GRC lead drafts a RACI chart for the review. Ana, a junior GRC analyst checking the draft, sees two managers marked Accountable and returns it to the GRC lead to settle which one answers for it.

review: Draft the chart with one proposed Accountable name per task
Update the chart's names when staff join, move or leave
evidence: Approved RACI chart with a version date
Organization chart showing the security leader's reporting line
audit_focus.recommend: Raise any task with no Accountable person, or several, with the GRC lead before approval.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management assigns accountability and approves reporting lines

subtopics.isaca_rule: One task, one accountable person. Work can be delegated; accountability cannot. When ownership is unclear, raise it so leadership assigns an owner, rather than quietly deciding yourself.

exam_traps.trap: Making two managers jointly accountable doubles the oversight.
exam_traps.why: Each assumes the other is acting. One person answers for each task; others can be Responsible or Consulted.

exam_traps.trap: Delegating a task to IT also hands IT the accountability.
exam_traps.why: IT becomes Responsible for the work, but the owner who delegated it still answers for the result.

key_terms.definition: Being answerable for an outcome; it stays with the owner even when tasks are delegated.
The path by which a role reports results and issues to the person or body above it.

subtopics.name: Compliance Obligations and Evidence
subtopics.definition: Compliance means meeting the requirements that apply to the organization, from laws and contracts to its own policies, and being able to prove it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Missing an obligation can bring fines, lost contracts and lost trust. Regulators and customers want records, not promises, so evidence matters as much as the control.
how_it_works: Identify each obligation, its source and what it requires, then assign an owner.
Map each obligation to the controls that meet it; one control can cover several.
Collect evidence as work happens, such as logs, tickets and test results.
Check on a schedule, and track each gap as a finding with an owner and due date.

rows.label: Example
cells: A privacy law such as the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) rules required by a payment provider
A rule that every laptop uses full-disk encryption

rows.label: Optional?
cells: No, for the staff it covers

subtopics.example: A dental practice's booking contract requires suspected data breaches to be reported within 48 hours, and health privacy law adds its own deadlines; both go on the obligations list. When Kai, the IT assistant, later sees an unusual login to the booking system, Kai starts the incident procedure at once, knowing the reporting clock may be running.

review: Map each obligation you log to its owner and a control
Report missing or late evidence to the control owner
evidence: Dated sign-offs for approved changes
Open findings list with owners and due dates
audit_focus.recommend: Tell the control owner as soon as evidence is missing or a deadline is at risk.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management decides how and when a compliance gap is closed

subtopics.isaca_rule: Compliance is proven, not claimed. Know where each obligation comes from, map it to a control and keep the evidence. A voluntary framework never replaces a legal or contract duty.

exam_traps.trap: Passing last year's audit means the organization is still compliant.
exam_traps.why: Compliance is ongoing. Systems, laws and controls change, so an old audit shows only the state at that time.

exam_traps.trap: Following a respected framework satisfies every legal requirement.
exam_traps.why: Frameworks are voluntary guidance. Laws and contracts can demand specific things, such as breach-notice deadlines, that a framework never mentions.

key_terms.definition: Records that show a control operated, such as logs, tickets, approvals or test results.
A documented gap between a requirement and what actually happens, with an owner and a fix date.

subtopics.name: Choosing and Mapping Frameworks in GRC
subtopics.definition: Mapping frameworks means linking a governance, risk and compliance (GRC) program's own controls to each framework it must show progress against.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Customers, regulators and leaders often ask about different frameworks. Mapping one control set to all of them avoids a second program and shows the real gaps.
how_it_works: Start from what leaders, customers or contracts ask to see; 1.3.3 covers what each framework contains.
Load the framework into the GRC tool, then link each control to the items it meets.
A crosswalk maps one framework to another, so one control shows progress against both.
Tailor it: mark items that do not apply and record why.

types.meaning: Describes results to reach, not how. Suits progress reports to leaders.
Lists specific safeguards in priority order. Suits choosing first steps.
Sets requirements an accredited body can audit and certify. Suits customers who want formal proof.

subtopics.example: A credit union follows ISO/IEC 27001, an international security management standard, and a major customer asks for progress against the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF). Instead of a second program, the GRC lead builds a crosswalk in the GRC tool. Kofi, a junior analyst, maps each control to a CSF outcome and flags three outcomes with no control for review.

review: Update control mappings when a framework issues a new version
Record the reason each time you mark an item not applicable
evidence: Mapping export showing each control's linked framework items
Statement of applicability with reasons for exclusions
audit_focus.recommend: Send unexplained exclusions or stale mappings to the GRC lead for a recorded decision.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management chooses the frameworks and approves tailoring

subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose frameworks by need, map controls once and reuse the evidence. Tailoring is expected, but every exclusion needs a recorded reason.

exam_traps.trap: A framework must be adopted in full, or it is not really being followed.
exam_traps.why: Frameworks expect tailoring to an organization's risks and size, with a documented reason for each choice.

exam_traps.trap: Adopting a second framework means building a second set of controls.
exam_traps.why: A crosswalk maps one control set to several frameworks, so one control can show progress against both. Only real gaps need new controls.

key_terms.definition: A mapping that shows how items in one framework or standard match items in another.
A document listing which controls of a standard apply, whether each is in place, and why any are excluded.

subtopics.name: GRC Tools and Automation
subtopics.definition: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) tools are platforms that keep risks, controls, policies and evidence in one place and automate routine tasks.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Spreadsheets and email chains break as programs grow. A tool gives one current record, but only if owners keep it accurate and act on it.
how_it_works: Risk and control modules link each risk to its owner and the controls that treat it.
Policy management tracks versions, approvals and staff acknowledgments.
Automated collection pulls settings from systems on a schedule and flags any control that drifts.
Dashboards turn the stored data into views for each audience.
A status is only as current as its data; check when each feed last updated before trusting a green.
subtopics.example: A freight company's GRC platform has shown its server patching control as green for three months. Yuki, a junior GRC analyst, opens the record and sees the patch server's data feed stopped in July, when its service account password expired, so the green rests on an old export. Yuki marks the control's status as unverified, tells the control owner and raises a ticket for the platform owner to repair the feed.

review: Check the live setting on the system before acting on an alert
Link the corrected setting to its change record
evidence: Alert history showing when the control drifted
Configuration export taken after the fix
audit_focus.recommend: Pass alerts outside your permissions to the control owner; never edit the monitoring rule yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The control owner decides how a monitored control is set

subtopics.isaca_rule: A tool supports governance but never replaces it. When it flags a gap, confirm it, act within the procedure and leave a record; never silence the alert.

exam_traps.trap: Once the GRC platform is installed, compliance is automatic.
exam_traps.why: Tools collect and display data. People still decide risk treatment, approve policies and fix gaps.

exam_traps.trap: Turn off a noisy alert so the dashboard shows green.
exam_traps.why: Hiding an alert hides the risk. Confirm whether it is real, then fix it or ask the control owner to tune the rule.

key_terms.definition: Automated, frequent checks that a control is still in its expected state, with alerts when it drifts.
One agreed, current record that everyone uses instead of separate copies.

subtopics.name: Tolerances and the Risk Register in GRC
subtopics.definition: In a governance, risk and compliance (GRC) program, the risk register links each risk to a tolerance, an owner, its controls and an indicator.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Statements such as "little risk with customer data" do not say when to act. GRC turns them into numbers, so a risk that leaves its limit is noticed.
how_it_works: Appetite, tolerance and acceptance are introduced in 1.2.6; here a GRC program puts them to work.
Tolerances become the thresholds on key risk indicators (KRIs), so a dashboard shows when a risk leaves its limit.
Each entry links to the controls that treat the risk, so a failed control changes its status.
Risks above tolerance go to senior management; accepted risks carry a reason and a review date.

columns: Risk register in a GRC program

rows.label: Tolerance
cells: A measurable limit for each risk

rows.label: Links to controls
cells: Each risk linked to the controls that treat it

rows.label: Warning
cells: A KRI threshold alerts the risk owner

rows.label: Review
cells: On a set cycle and after major changes

subtopics.example: A ticketing company's GRC platform links the risk "card data stored where it should not be" to a KRI: card files found outside the payment system, with a tolerance of zero. A weekly scan finds two on a shared drive. Lena, a junior analyst, confirms they hold real card numbers and logs the finding against the register entry, moving the risk above tolerance.

review: Keep each entry's tolerance, owner and review date current
Compare current indicator values with each tolerance
evidence: Register history showing who changed a rating, and when
Signed risk acceptance with a reason and expiry date
audit_focus.recommend: Log new facts against the register entry, and alert the risk owner when a risk leaves tolerance.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner accepts risk within tolerance; senior management decides above it

subtopics.isaca_rule: A risk is managed only when it has a measurable tolerance, an owner, linked controls and an indicator. Practitioners keep the register accurate and never accept risk themselves.

exam_traps.trap: A risk appetite statement is enough; teams can judge each risk against it by feel.
exam_traps.why: Broad statements need measurable tolerances and thresholds, or two teams will judge the same risk differently. GRC turns appetite into numbers people can check.

exam_traps.trap: An accepted risk is closed for good.
exam_traps.why: Acceptance holds only while conditions hold, so every accepted risk carries a review date.

key_terms.definition: The risk left after controls are applied; the risk owner accepts it within tolerance, and only senior management can accept it above tolerance.
The agreed actions, owner and dates for bringing a risk back within tolerance.

subtopics.name: Governing AI Use
subtopics.definition: Governing artificial intelligence (AI) use means setting rules for which AI tools staff may use, for which tasks and with which data, and tracking every use.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Staff adopt AI assistants faster than policies appear, so nobody knows which tools hold company data or who owns each use.
how_it_works: An AI acceptable use policy (AUP), approved by senior management, sets the rules, including checking AI output before relying on it.
An approved tools list, kept as a standard under the policy, names vetted services and the data each may handle.
An AI inventory records each use and its owner; a new use is reviewed before it starts.
Pasting confidential data into public AI tools can leak it; 5.1.8 covers that risk.
The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) AI Risk Management Framework can structure this work.
Approval holds only while the facts behind it hold; a change in vendor terms, data or purpose sends the tool back for review.
subtopics.example: A city library's service owner ends a trial of an AI chatbot that answered borrowers' questions. Tomas, the IT support analyst who keeps the AI inventory, marks the entry retired, removes staff access and files the vendor's written confirmation that stored chats were deleted, as the contract requires.

review: Confirm a tool is approved before using it for work
Look for AI uses in your area missing from the inventory
evidence: Signed staff acknowledgments of the AI policy
Vendor terms on how each service keeps prompts
audit_focus.recommend: Report unapproved AI tools to the security team; do not block or approve them yourself.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management approves the AI policy and tools; data owners decide what data may be used

subtopics.isaca_rule: Use only approved AI tools, for approved purposes, with data the policy allows. Unapproved tools are a policy issue to report, not a shortcut to take.

exam_traps.trap: Once a tool is on the approved list, any work data may go into it.
exam_traps.why: Approval comes with limits: check the data's classification against what the list allows for that tool.

exam_traps.trap: Ban every AI tool so the risk disappears.
exam_traps.why: Blanket bans push staff toward hidden tools. Approved options, clear data rules and monitoring work better.

key_terms.definition: A list of where AI is used, who owns each use and what data it touches.
A list of vetted AI services, each with the data classification levels it may handle.

topics.overview: Redundancy keeps services running when a part fails, and continuity and recovery plans cover the failures redundancy cannot absorb. This topic covers business continuity (BC) and disaster recovery (DR), the business impact analysis (BIA) and recovery targets behind them, backups, recovery sites, plan testing, and what changes when services depend on AI.
can_do: Tell business continuity from disaster recovery, and redundancy from backup
Use the recovery time objective (RTO), recovery point objective (RPO) and maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) to judge a backup schedule or recovery site
Put the five plan test types in order from least to most disruptive
Explain why AI models, settings and datasets need backups, and why model drift is a continuity risk

subtopics.name: Redundancy and High Availability
subtopics.definition: Redundancy means having spare components, paths or copies ready to take over when one fails, so one failure does not stop a service.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Hardware breaks, power drops and cables get cut. Removing single points of failure protects availability, the "A" in the confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA) triad.
how_it_works: Find single points of failure, such as one server, one internet link or one key person.
Add a spare for each; failover moves work to it, automatically or by procedure.
High availability (HA) combines redundancy and failover so users notice little or no outage.
Put spares in another building or region when a whole site could be lost.

types.meaning: A redundant array of independent disks (RAID) that writes the same data to two disks; either disk can fail without data loss.
Spreads data and recovery information across three or more disks; survives the loss of any one disk.
Several servers work as one; if one fails, another takes over its work.
Spreads requests across several servers, so losing one reduces capacity instead of stopping service.
An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) bridges short outages with batteries; a generator covers longer ones.
Two internet providers or paths, so one cut cable does not cut the service.

subtopics.example: A warehouse runs its order system on one server and one internet line. After a storm cuts the line for a day, the operations manager approves a second line from another provider and a standby server that takes over automatically. Ben, a junior technician, tests the switch-over monthly as the runbook sets out and logs each result.

review: Confirm the spare takes over during a scheduled test
Mark known single points of failure on the network diagrams
evidence: Failover test log with dates and outcome
Current diagram of power and network paths
audit_focus.recommend: Log any untested or missing spare and pass it to the system owner.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner decides which redundancy to fund

subtopics.isaca_rule: Redundancy protects availability against component failure; backups protect against loss and corruption. When data is deleted, corrupted or encrypted, redundancy is not the fix.

exam_traps.trap: RAID or a mirrored server means we do not need backups.
exam_traps.why: Mirroring copies every change, including deletions and ransomware, the malicious software (malware) that encrypts files for a ransom. Only an earlier, separate copy helps.

exam_traps.trap: Two servers in the same rack give full protection.
exam_traps.why: A fire, flood or power cut takes out both. Distance between copies matters for site-wide events.

key_terms.definition: One component whose failure stops a whole service because nothing can take its place.
Switching work from a failed component to its standby.

subtopics.name: Business Continuity vs Disaster Recovery
subtopics.definition: Business continuity (BC) keeps critical business functions running during a disruption; disaster recovery (DR) restores the technology and data those functions depend on.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Restored servers are useless if staff have nowhere to work. Treating DR as the whole of BC leaves people, places and processes unplanned.
how_it_works: The BC plan covers the whole business, including people, workplaces and suppliers.
The DR plan is the technical part: restoring systems and data, often at an alternate site.
Both start from the business impact analysis (BIA) and name who may declare a disaster.
Human safety comes first: account for people before saving equipment or data.

rows.label: Main goal
cells: Detect, contain and recover from a security incident

rows.label: Typical trigger
cells: Any major disruption: fire, pandemic, supplier failure
Loss of a data center, system or data
A security event that harms or threatens assets

rows.label: Example action
cells: Staff work from a second office
Restore servers at a recovery site

subtopics.example: A flood closes a call center overnight. IT restores the phone and ticket systems in the cloud within hours, which is disaster recovery, but no one planned where agents would sit. Maya, a support analyst, follows the call tree, checks in with her team lead and waits for instructions instead of driving to the closed site.

review: Confirm your contact details in the call tree are current
Note plan sections that cover systems but not people
evidence: Approved plan naming who may activate it
Actions from the last plan review
audit_focus.recommend: Send outdated contacts or missing roles to the business continuity manager before the next test.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management or a named crisis lead declares a disaster

subtopics.isaca_rule: Disaster recovery is one part of business continuity, not all of it. Plan for people, places, suppliers and communication as well as systems, and put people's safety before any asset.

exam_traps.trap: Our disaster recovery plan is our business continuity plan.
exam_traps.why: DR restores technology. BC also covers staff, workspace, suppliers and communication.

exam_traps.trap: During a fire, grab the backup drives on the way out.
exam_traps.why: Life safety comes first. Backups are kept offsite so no one has to risk injury to save data.

key_terms.definition: A set list of who contacts whom, in order, to alert staff during a disruption.
The formal decision by an authorized person to activate the recovery plan.

subtopics.name: Business Impact Analysis (BIA)
subtopics.definition: A business impact analysis (BIA) identifies an organization's critical functions, what each depends on and how harm grows over time if each one stops.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The BIA decides what is recovered first and how fast. Every later choice, from backup schedule to recovery site, rests on it.
how_it_works: List business functions, such as taking orders or paying staff, before listing systems.
Function owners rate how harm grows at several outage lengths.
Record what each function depends on, such as systems, people and suppliers.
Set each function's maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) and recovery targets, then rank functions; senior management approves the results.

rows.label: Main question
cells: If this function stops, how bad is it over time?
What could go wrong, and how likely is it?

subtopics.example: A university's BIA team asks the registrar how long course enrollment can stop in the first week of term: a few hours, while the alumni newsletter can wait a month. Leo, a help desk analyst helping with the survey, adds an outside payment provider to enrollment's dependency list when a staff member mentions it.

review: Update a function's dependency list when it adds a supplier
Draft the restore order from the BIA's approved priorities
evidence: Owner-confirmed impact ratings at several outage lengths
Signed approval page for the current BIA
audit_focus.recommend: Pass missing functions or dependencies to the business continuity manager for the next update.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management signs off which functions recover first

subtopics.isaca_rule: The BIA starts from business functions and their owners, not from IT's server list, and it comes before choosing recovery sites or backup schedules.

exam_traps.trap: Begin the BIA by rating how important each server is.
exam_traps.why: Servers matter only because functions depend on them. Starting from servers misses people, suppliers and manual steps.

exam_traps.trap: The BIA is mainly about how likely each disaster is.
exam_traps.why: The BIA measures impact over time. Likelihood belongs to the risk assessment.

key_terms.definition: A business activity whose loss would quickly cause serious harm, so it is restored first.
Anything a function needs to run, such as a system, data set, person, site or supplier.

subtopics.name: Recovery Objectives: MTD, RTO and RPO
subtopics.definition: Recovery objectives are limits set by the business: how long a function can be down and how much recent data it can afford to lose.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These numbers drive cost: a shorter downtime target needs a readier site, and a smaller data-loss target needs more frequent copies.
how_it_works: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), also called maximum tolerable period of disruption, is the longest a function can be out before harm is unacceptable.
Recovery time objective (RTO) is the target time to restore the function; it must fit within the MTD.
Recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, the business can lose; it looks back from the disruption.
Business owners set these in the business impact analysis (BIA); IT designs solutions to meet them.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: How long before the outage is intolerable?
How fast must we be running again?
How much recent data can we lose?

rows.label: Direction
cells: Backward to the last good copy

rows.label: What meets it
cells: Not met directly; the RTO must fit inside it
Recovery site, staff and tested procedures

subtopics.example: A veterinary clinic backs up its booking system nightly, but the practice manager says losing more than an hour of appointments would be serious. Noor, a junior technician, sees that the backup can lose up to 24 hours of bookings, far beyond the one-hour RPO, and raises the gap with the IT lead.

review: Line up actual copy times against each data-loss target
Time a test restore against the downtime target
evidence: Backup job logs showing when copies ran
BIA record with owner-approved MTD, RTO and RPO
audit_focus.recommend: Report missed targets to the system owner with the numbers, without changing the schedule or target.
audit_focus.decides: Business owners set the targets; senior management funds any gap

subtopics.isaca_rule: RPO is about data, looking back; RTO is about time, looking forward; the RTO must fit inside the MTD. A hot site shortens downtime but does nothing for data loss.

exam_traps.trap: A faster recovery site will reduce how much data we lose.
exam_traps.why: Site readiness affects the RTO. Only more frequent backups or replication improve the RPO.

exam_traps.trap: IT should set the RTO to whatever current systems can achieve.
exam_traps.why: Targets come from business impact. If IT cannot meet one, that is a gap to report and fund.

key_terms.definition: Time after systems return to check data and clear backlog; RTO plus WRT must fit inside the MTD.
Copying data to another site continuously or nearly so, supporting a very small RPO.

subtopics.memory_aid: RPO: the Point you roll back to. RTO: the Time until you are running. MTD: the hard limit.

subtopics.name: Backups: Types, the 3-2-1 Rule and Restore Testing
subtopics.definition: A backup is a separate copy of data, and often of settings, kept so the original can be restored after loss, corruption or attack.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Backups are the last defense against ransomware and mistakes. A backup never restored is a hope, not a control, and one attackers can reach may be encrypted too.
how_it_works: Choose the backup type and frequency to meet the recovery point objective (RPO).
Follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, on two types of storage, with one offsite.
Keep at least one copy offline or immutable, so ransomware or a stolen admin account cannot change it.
Test restores on a schedule and time them against the recovery time objective (RTO).

types.meaning: Copies all selected data every time. Slowest to make and simplest to restore: one set.
Copies only what changed since the last backup of any kind. Fast to make; a restore needs the last full plus every incremental since, in order.
Copies everything changed since the last full backup. Grows each day; a restore needs the last full plus only the latest differential.
A quick point-in-time image of a system or volume. Useful, but often stored on the same system, so not a backup on its own.
