subtopics.example: A broadband provider backs up nightly to a storage unit beside its server and also syncs its files to a cloud folder. Nadia, an IT assistant checking the setup against the 3-2-1 rule, points out that a synced folder is not a backup: it copies every change, so files encrypted by ransomware would sync there too. The system owner approves adding a nightly immutable cloud copy, kept for 30 days.

review: Restore a sample of files and time the result
Compare backed-up systems with the asset inventory
evidence: Restore test record with date and time taken
Storage settings showing a retention lock
audit_focus.recommend: Report failed restores or unprotected backup copies to the system owner the same day.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner decides backup scope and retention, within policy

subtopics.isaca_rule: A backup counts only if it can be restored in time and attackers cannot reach it. Look for separation (offsite, offline or immutable) and proven restores.

exam_traps.trap: Backups run every night with no errors, so recovery is assured.
exam_traps.why: A successful job shows data was copied. Corrupt files or a slow restore show up only when you restore and time it.

exam_traps.trap: An incremental restore needs only the full and the latest incremental.
exam_traps.why: That is the differential rule. A restore from incrementals needs the full plus every incremental since, in order.

key_terms.definition: A backup that cannot be changed or deleted, even by an administrator, until its retention period ends.
A copy disconnected from networks, sometimes called air-gapped, so remote attackers cannot reach it.

subtopics.name: Recovery Sites
subtopics.definition: A recovery site is an alternate place to run critical systems or work when the main site is unusable, from an empty room to a running copy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The site must match the recovery time objective (RTO). Too slow misses the target; too ready wastes money on standby equipment.
how_it_works: Readier sites recover faster and cost more to keep ready.
Match the site to the RTO from the business impact analysis (BIA), not to habit or budget.
Keep it far enough away that one regional event, such as a flood, cannot hit both sites.
Cloud recovery means paying mainly for stored copies until a failover, and it still needs testing.
Give the recovery site the same security controls as the main site, including monitoring, from the moment it runs.

rows.label: What is ready
cells: Equipment and connections; data must be restored
Stored copies; computing started on demand

rows.label: Typical recovery time
cells: Minutes to hours, if built and tested

rows.label: Fits an RTO of
cells: About a day to a few days

subtopics.example: An online pharmacy's BIA sets a four-hour RTO for orders. To save money, finance proposes a cold site across town. Sana, a junior analyst preparing the options, notes that a cold site takes days to equip and sits in the same flood zone. She puts both facts in the comparison before the decision.

review: Compare each site option's recovery time with the RTO
Confirm the site sits outside the main site's regional hazards
evidence: Latest failover test record with time to full operation
Site contract stating capacity and readiness
audit_focus.recommend: Present site options against the RTO to the business continuity manager, flagging any that fall short.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management chooses and funds the recovery site

subtopics.isaca_rule: Let the RTO pick the site: hours means hot or a tested cloud setup, days means warm, weeks means cold. A cheaper site that misses the RTO is not a saving.

exam_traps.trap: A cold site is fine for a four-hour RTO, because it is cheaper.
exam_traps.why: A cold site has no equipment or data, so it takes days or weeks to bring up. It cannot meet an RTO in hours.

exam_traps.trap: Moving to the cloud means recovery is automatic.
exam_traps.why: Cloud recovery still needs copies in another region and tested procedures; the customer still owns its data and settings.

key_terms.definition: A deal where two organizations host each other's work in a disaster; cheap but hard to rely on.
A provider service that copies systems to its cloud and runs them there during a disaster.

subtopics.name: Testing and Maintaining BC and DR Plans
subtopics.definition: Plan testing checks that business continuity (BC) and disaster recovery (DR) plans work and that people know their roles.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An untested plan fails at the worst moment, with wrong numbers, missing steps and slow restores. Testing finds this while it is cheap to fix.
how_it_works: Start with low-risk tests and move to more realistic ones as the plan matures.
Set goals for each test, such as meeting the recovery time objective (RTO), and record the results.
Update the plan after every test, real event and major change; senior management approves disruptive tests.
Incident response exercises (5.3.7) use a similar ladder, from tabletop to full-scale; a tabletop is the same discussion-based test in both.

types.meaning: Each team reviews the plan on its own for errors and outdated details. No disruption.
Team members meet and talk through a scenario step by step. No systems are touched.
Teams act out their roles in a realistic scenario, sometimes on test systems, without stopping production.
Systems are brought up at the recovery site and run alongside production, which keeps running.
Production is shut down and the business runs from the recovery site. Most realistic and highest risk.

subtopics.example: A city water department runs a parallel test of its billing system, bringing it up at the recovery site while production keeps running. The restore takes nine hours against a six-hour RTO. Dee, a junior system administrator, records each step's timing in the test report, and the gap becomes a tracked action.

review: Confirm your role and contact details before each test
Compare results with the targets the test aimed to meet
evidence: Lessons-learned actions with owners and due dates
Plan version history showing post-test updates
audit_focus.recommend: Send test gaps to the plan owner and track them until the plan is updated.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management decides whether production may be shut down

subtopics.isaca_rule: Test in order of risk: checklist, tabletop, simulation, parallel, full interruption. Choose the least disruptive test that meets the goal; a full interruption needs senior management approval.

exam_traps.trap: Start testing a new plan with a full interruption, the most realistic test.
exam_traps.why: It can cause the very outage the plan is meant to handle. Find basic errors first with checklists and tabletops.

exam_traps.trap: A parallel test shuts down production to prove the recovery site works.
exam_traps.why: In a parallel test production keeps running. Shutting it down is a full interruption test.

key_terms.definition: A review after a test or event that records what worked, what did not and who will fix each gap.
Regular updates that keep a plan in step with changes in staff, systems, suppliers and sites.

subtopics.name: Backing Up AI Systems and Model Drift
subtopics.definition: Resilience for artificial intelligence (AI) services means being able to restore the models, settings and data behind them, and noticing when performance declines.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An AI service can fail while its servers are up: the model may be lost, misconfigured or slowly getting worse. If a process depends on it, that is a continuity risk.
how_it_works: Back up what rebuilds the service: model versions, settings and prompts, and the training data.
Version these backups, so a known-good model and its settings restore together.
Model drift is a gradual drop in accuracy as real-world data moves away from what the model learned.
Plan a fallback, such as an earlier model version or a manual process.
subtopics.example: A delivery firm's AI model predicts late parcels, and dispatchers plan routes around it. After the firm adds a new region, accuracy slips week by week. Kim, a junior operations analyst, sees the weekly figure fall below the agreed threshold and reports it to the model owner, who switches dispatch back to the previous model version.

review: Confirm the AI backup set includes model, settings and data
Note outside AI providers the service depends on
evidence: Versioned backup records for model files
Documented fallback procedure for the AI service
audit_focus.recommend: Report drift alerts to the model owner with the figures and dates, rather than retraining the model yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides whether to roll back, retrain or pause

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat an AI service like any critical system: back up everything needed to rebuild it and plan a fallback. A model can fail slowly while every server looks healthy.

exam_traps.trap: Backing up the training data is enough to recover an AI service.
exam_traps.why: Without the exact model version, settings and prompts, you may not rebuild the same behavior, and retraining can take days.

exam_traps.trap: If the AI servers are up, the AI service is available.
exam_traps.why: A drifting model that gives wrong answers is effectively down for the process that relies on it.

key_terms.definition: Returning a system to an earlier, known-good version after a problem.
The person accountable for an AI model's purpose, performance and approved changes.

subtopics.name: AI-Assisted Detection and Resilience
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) assisted detection spots trouble early; for resilience, it must catch events before they disrupt the business and keep working through an outage.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An attack caught early may never need the recovery plan. But monitoring that sits on the failed systems leaves the organization blind when most exposed.
how_it_works: AI monitoring flags early warning signs, such as files renamed at high speed just before ransomware encrypts them.
Activation triggers, such as confirmed ransomware spread, move a response from incident handling into continuity or recovery.
Run monitoring where a main-site failure cannot take it down, and restore it early.
Back up detection rules, settings and logs away from the monitored systems. Alert triage itself is taught in 5.2.3.
subtopics.example: A logistics firm's AI monitoring tool flags files on the shipping server being renamed at high speed, an early sign of ransomware. The playbook tells Jo, the night-shift analyst, to confirm it in the logs and call the on-call incident response lead, who has the server isolated before the encryption spreads. Because it was caught early, the firm never has to declare a disaster or fail over to its recovery site.

review: Confirm monitoring appears in the recovery plan's restore order
Ask the system owner where the monitoring tool is hosted
evidence: Recovery plan section covering monitoring at the recovery site
Last good copy of the monitoring tool's configuration
audit_focus.recommend: Raise monitoring gaps at the recovery site with the business continuity manager before the next test.
audit_focus.decides: The incident response lead decides containment; senior management declares a disaster

subtopics.isaca_rule: Early detection is a resilience control: the sooner an event is caught, the less there is to recover. Detection must survive the outage it warns about.

exam_traps.trap: During a disaster, security monitoring can wait until normal systems are back.
exam_traps.why: Attackers exploit confusion, and restored systems are exposed too. Monitoring belongs early in the restore order.

exam_traps.trap: Restoring the servers also restores everything the detection tool knew.
exam_traps.why: Only if its rules, settings and logs were backed up separately. Logs left on encrypted servers are lost.

key_terms.definition: Detection soon enough to contain an event before it disrupts a critical business function.
A defined condition, such as confirmed ransomware spread, that starts the continuity or recovery plan.

topics.overview: Most attacks reach people before they reach systems. This topic covers building a culture where security matters and leaders model it, and the core ideas every staff member needs: social engineering, phishing, including AI-generated lures, and protecting passwords. A safe, fast reporting habit ties it all together.
can_do: Explain how leadership and a no-blame reporting culture make awareness work
Tell awareness, training and education apart and match each to an audience
Spot the pressure tactics in a social engineering or phishing scenario, including AI-generated lures
Build safe password habits: long, unique passphrases, a password manager, no sharing and fast reporting

subtopics.name: Security Culture and Leadership
subtopics.definition: Security culture is the shared attitudes and habits that shape how people treat security day to day, especially when no one is watching.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls fail when people work around them. A culture where staff value security and feel safe reporting mistakes catches problems early.
how_it_works: Leaders set the tone: they follow the same rules, talk about security and fund it.
Security is part of everyone's job, not only the security team's.
Reporting is easy and safe, with thanks instead of blame for honest mistakes.
Culture is judged by behavior, such as reporting rates, not course completion.
subtopics.example: At a regional bus operator, the chief executive tells an all-staff meeting about clicking a phishing link last month, reporting it within minutes and being thanked by the security team. Over the next quarter, staff reports of suspicious messages double. Jamal, a new security analyst, adds the report rate to the culture measures shared with leaders each month.

review: Follow the same rules you ask others to follow
Record exception requests instead of granting them informally
evidence: Exception register with approver, reason and expiry date
Staff survey results on willingness to report
audit_focus.recommend: Route every exception request, including those from senior leaders, through the documented exception process to the policy owner.
audit_focus.decides: The policy owner approves exceptions; senior management decides any risk above tolerance

subtopics.isaca_rule: Culture starts at the top and grows through safe reporting. Leadership support and no-blame reporting do more than extra technology or punishment. Exceptions go through the formal process, whoever asks.

exam_traps.trap: Punishing staff who click phishing links will improve security.
exam_traps.why: Fear makes people hide mistakes, and hidden incidents grow. Fast reports matter more than any single click.

exam_traps.trap: Security culture is the security team's job.
exam_traps.why: Culture comes from leaders and everyday behavior. Without leadership backing, awareness efforts fade.

key_terms.definition: The example leaders set through their own behavior and priorities, which staff tend to follow.
A recorded, time-limited permission to depart from a policy, approved by the policy owner and reviewed before it expires.

subtopics.name: Awareness, Training and Education
subtopics.definition: Awareness keeps security in mind for everyone, training builds job-specific skills for particular roles, and education builds deeper understanding for those whose careers need it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One course for everyone wastes time and misses real risks. A developer, a payroll clerk and a help desk agent face different attacks.
how_it_works: Awareness reaches everyone through short, frequent messages, such as reminders and brief campaigns.
Basic training happens at onboarding and then on a regular cycle, such as yearly.
Role-based training adds what a job needs: secure coding for developers, caller checks for the help desk.
Content is refreshed as threats change, for example to cover scams written with artificial intelligence (AI).

rows.label: Example
cells: Help desk staff practice verifying callers

subtopics.example: An online travel agency gives every employee the same yearly course, yet code scans keep finding the same injection flaw in booking forms its developers write. The awareness lead adds a hands-on secure coding module for the developers, keeps short monthly reminders for everyone and tracks the scan results to see whether the module works.

review: Confirm you completed the training your role requires
Compare the mistakes you see with what training covers
evidence: Training records by role, with dates
Role-to-course mapping showing who needs which module
audit_focus.recommend: Pass patterns of repeated mistakes to the awareness lead so role-based content can be added.
audit_focus.decides: Management sets the training each role requires

subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the learning to the role and the risk. Everyone gets awareness; higher-risk roles get role-based training on top. When one group repeats one mistake, train that group.

exam_traps.trap: Give everyone the same annual course so training is fair.
exam_traps.why: Roles that handle money, access or code face specific attacks and need training on them, on top of the basics.

exam_traps.trap: A completed course means staff will behave securely.
exam_traps.why: Completion shows attendance, not behavior. Measure behavior, such as phishing report rates.

key_terms.definition: Training built for the duties and risks of a specific job, given on top of general awareness.
Preparing new staff, including security training before or soon after they get access.

subtopics.name: Social Engineering Tactics
subtopics.definition: Social engineering is manipulating people into giving up information, access or money by exploiting trust, fear, helpfulness or urgency instead of technical flaws.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It is often easier to trick a person than to break a system. One convinced employee can hand over what firewalls and access controls protect.
how_it_works: Attackers research targets through social media, company websites and earlier data leaks.
They build a believable story, such as a new IT contractor or a supplier.
They apply pressure, such as authority, urgency or the wish to help, and ask for one small step.
The defense: slow down, verify through a separate known channel and follow procedure.
At a badge door, never let in anyone who cannot badge in, whatever uniform or ID card they show; send them to reception to sign in.

types.meaning: Using an invented story and role to win trust and draw out information.
Posing as a real or plausible person, such as a manager, supplier or IT staff member.
Tailgating is following someone through a controlled door without their knowledge or consent; piggybacking is the same with their knowledge or consent, such as when they hold it open.
Leaving a tempting item, such as a memory stick labeled "salaries", for someone to pick up and use.
Offering a favor, such as free tech help, in exchange for access or information.
Watching someone type a password or read sensitive data on screen.

subtopics.example: A caller claiming to be from the district's IT supplier tells a school receptionist that email will shut down within the hour unless they get the principal's login. The receptionist takes the caller's name, hangs up and rings the IT desk on the staff directory number to check the story.

review: Verify unusual requests through a known number or in person
Log the time, caller details and request made
evidence: Official contact list used for call-backs
Visitor and badge logs for in-person attempts
audit_focus.recommend: Report every suspected social engineering attempt to the security team, including the ones you stopped.
audit_focus.decides: The security team decides whether to warn other staff

subtopics.isaca_rule: Pressure is the signal. When a request is urgent, unusual or backed by authority, verify it through a channel you already trust, not one the requester supplies, and report every attempt.

exam_traps.trap: The caller knew the manager's name and the project, so the request is genuine.
exam_traps.why: Those details come from public sources and earlier contacts. Knowing internal facts proves research, not identity.

exam_traps.trap: Verify a caller by calling back the number they give you.
exam_traps.why: The attacker controls that number. Use the staff directory or the official website instead.

key_terms.definition: Confirming a request through a separate, trusted channel, such as a known phone number, instead of replying to it.
Information gathered from public sources, such as social media, often used to make a story convincing.

subtopics.name: Phishing and Its Variants
subtopics.definition: Phishing is a message, usually an email, text or call, that pretends to come from a trusted source to trick the reader into clicking, sharing data or paying.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Phishing is one of the most common ways attackers steal passwords and trigger fraudulent payments. Fast reporting protects the whole organization.
how_it_works: Lures copy trusted senders, such as a bank, a delivery firm or the IT team.
Warning signs include urgency, requests for passwords or payment, and addresses that do not match.
Hover over links to see where they go, and type known addresses yourself.
Report it with the approved button; do not forward it. If you clicked, report at once.

types.meaning: Targets a specific person or team, using personal details to look genuine.
Spear phishing aimed at senior executives or other high-value people.
Uses a real or faked business email account to request payments or changes to bank details.
Phishing by text message (SMS, short message service).
Phishing by voice call, including recorded or artificially generated voices.
Phishing through a QR (quick response) code that leads to a fake website.

subtopics.example: A logistics clerk gets an email, seemingly from the company's delivery software, warning that their account locks today unless they sign in through a link. The sender's address is slightly misspelled. The clerk does not click or forward it to coworkers. They use the report button, then open the real software from their bookmarks to check the account.

review: Inspect the sender address and link destination before acting
Tell the security team at once if you clicked or signed in
evidence: Message headers showing the real sending address
Sign-in history for the targeted account
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected phishing to the security team and leave blocking or removal decisions to them.
audit_focus.decides: The security team decides whether to remove the message company-wide

subtopics.isaca_rule: Do not click, do not reply, report. A suspicious message goes to the approved reporting channel, not the trash or a colleague's inbox, and anyone who clicked reports it immediately.

exam_traps.trap: Delete a suspicious email so no one else clicks it.
exam_traps.why: Deleting hides the attack from the security team, who may need to remove the same message from other inboxes.

exam_traps.trap: The email has the company logo and the right name, so it is safe.
exam_traps.why: Logos and names are easy to copy. Check the sender, the link and whether the request makes sense.

key_terms.definition: Faking the sender details of a message so it appears to come from someone else.
Collecting usernames and passwords through a fake sign-in page.

subtopics.name: AI-Boosted Phishing and Deepfakes
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) boosted social engineering uses AI tools to write convincing messages, clone voices or fake video, making scams more personal and more plentiful.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Old warning signs such as poor grammar are fading. Attackers can copy an executive's writing or voice, so people must rely on verification, not on how genuine something seems.
how_it_works: Generative AI writes fluent, personalized lures in many languages, at scale.
Voice cloning copies a voice from a short recording; deepfake video puts a familiar face on a live call.
Defenses rely on process: call-backs to known numbers, code phrases and dual approval for payments.
Awareness content shows real AI examples to prove polish is no longer a clue, and teaches verifying requests through known channels.
subtopics.example: A recruitment agency's records coordinator takes a call in what sounds exactly like the managing director's voice, asking for a candidate's file to be emailed to a personal address. Staff agreed a code phrase for unusual requests. The caller cannot give it, so the coordinator sends nothing and reports the call, a likely AI voice clone, to the security team.

review: Verify payment requests by calling a known number
Confirm a second approver signed off any new payee
evidence: Call-back record with the number used and the outcome
Recording or screenshot of the suspicious call
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected AI-generated scams to the security team so training and warnings can be updated.
audit_focus.decides: Finance management sets payment approval and call-back rules

subtopics.isaca_rule: If sight and sound can be faked, procedure is the safeguard. Verify requests for money, passwords or access through a separate known channel, whoever seems to be asking.

exam_traps.trap: The message has perfect grammar and the right tone, so it is not phishing.
exam_traps.why: AI removes the errors people were taught to spot. Judge and verify the request, not the writing.

exam_traps.trap: You saw the executive on video, so the payment request is genuine.
exam_traps.why: Deepfakes can imitate real people on live calls. The call-back and normal approvals still apply.

key_terms.definition: Using AI to copy a person's voice from recordings so it can say new things.
A control where two authorized people must approve an action, such as a payment, before it happens.

subtopics.name: Password and Passphrase Habits
subtopics.definition: Password protection, for users, means choosing long, unique passphrases, keeping them in a password manager, never sharing them and reporting any exposure.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Reused passwords are a leading cause of account takeover. After one site is breached, attackers try the stolen passwords on many others.
how_it_works: Length beats complexity: a long passphrase is harder to guess than a short password with symbols. System-side rules are in 3.1.6.
Use a different password for every account, so one breach does not unlock the rest.
A password manager stores unique passwords; protect it with a strong passphrase and multifactor authentication (MFA).
Never share a password, even with IT or a manager, and report any exposure at once.

rows.label: Choosing
cells: A short word with a number and a symbol added
Several random words joined into a long passphrase

rows.label: Reuse
cells: One password for work and personal sites
A unique password for every account, kept in a password manager

rows.label: Sharing
cells: Telling IT or a manager who asks for it
Never sharing; IT can reset an account without knowing the password

rows.label: After a breach alert
cells: Waiting to see if anything happens
Reporting it and changing the password as the security team directs

subtopics.example: Dana, a youth sports league's volunteer coordinator, uses one password for the league email and a shopping site. After the shopping site is breached, attackers sign in to the league email and message parents. The league's IT volunteer reports it to the board and helps Dana set up a password manager, unique passphrases and app-based MFA.

review: Fix any work account the password manager flags as reused
Check breach alerts for your work email address
evidence: Password manager report of reused or weak passwords
Breach alert notices for your work accounts
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected password exposure to the security team at once and change the password as they direct.
audit_focus.decides: Security management sets the password and MFA standard, within approved policy

subtopics.isaca_rule: Long, unique, kept in a password manager and never shared. IT never needs your password, and any sign of exposure is reported at once.

exam_traps.trap: Reusing one strong password on several sites is safe because it is hard to guess.
exam_traps.why: Strength does not help once a site leaks it. Attackers try leaked passwords everywhere.

exam_traps.trap: A password manager is risky because it keeps every password in one place.
exam_traps.why: It encrypts the vault and makes unique passwords practical. With a strong passphrase and MFA on it, it is the safer choice.

key_terms.definition: A password made of several words, long enough to resist guessing yet easy to remember.
An app that creates, stores and fills strong, unique passwords, protected by one main secret.
Trying usernames and passwords stolen in one breach on many other sites.

subtopics.name: Reporting Culture and Phishing Simulations
subtopics.definition: A reporting culture makes it quick and safe to report suspicious messages, mistakes or incidents; phishing simulations let staff practice spotting lures.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Security teams can act only on what they know. A fast report, even of one's own mistake, can stop an attack before it spreads.
how_it_works: Give people one simple way to report, then thank them and share the outcome.
Report your own mistakes at once; delay does more harm than the mistake.
Simulations are approved in advance, avoid lures that cause real distress and treat a click as a teaching moment, not grounds for punishment.
Track how many people report and how fast, not just how many click.
subtopics.example: A library assistant clicks a link about overdue fines and then notices the odd web address. Embarrassed, they consider saying nothing. Remembering the no-blame policy, they use the report button within minutes and call the help desk, so the security team can reset the password and block the site.

review: Confirm a simulation has written approval before it is sent
Share results by team, never by named individual
evidence: Report records showing time to first report
Simulation results by team: report rate and click rate
audit_focus.recommend: Send simulation results to the awareness lead by team, without naming or shaming individuals.
audit_focus.decides: Management approves simulation campaigns and how results are used

subtopics.isaca_rule: Report early, report always, including your own mistakes. A growing report rate is a sign of a healthy culture.

exam_traps.trap: After clicking a phishing link, close the browser and wait to see what happens.
exam_traps.why: Attackers act fast. An immediate report lets the team reset accounts and block the threat.

exam_traps.trap: A falling click rate is the only sign of a successful phishing program.
exam_traps.why: Click rates move with how hard the lure is. Report rate and time to report show whether people act.

key_terms.definition: An authorized fake phishing message sent to staff to practice spotting and reporting it.
The share of people who report a simulated or real phishing message.

topics.overview: Leaders cannot steer security they cannot see. This topic covers turning raw measurements into useful metrics, telling performance indicators from key risk indicators (KRIs), setting thresholds that trigger action, and presenting results through dashboards, scorecards and reports, including indicators for AI systems.
can_do: Tell a measure from a metric, and a key performance indicator (KPI) from a key risk indicator (KRI)
Classify a measure as implementation, effectiveness, efficiency or impact
Choose a dashboard, scorecard or report for a given audience and purpose
Name useful AI risk indicators, such as model accuracy, override rates and unapproved AI tool use

subtopics.name: Measures and Metrics: The Basics
subtopics.definition: A measure is a raw, quantified result, such as 940 of 1,000 laptops patched; a metric compares measures against a goal to show progress or risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without measurement, leaders fund security on instinct. Good metrics show what is improving, what is slipping and where to act.
how_it_works: Start from a goal, such as patching critical flaws quickly, then pick measures that show progress.
Collect data the same way every period, so trends mean something.
Compare each result with a baseline and a target.
If a metric drives no decision, drop it; a few meaningful metrics beat many.
subtopics.example: A city council's IT team reports "12,000 threats blocked this month", and councilors cannot tell whether that is good. The security lead switches to "critical patches applied within 14 days: 78%, target 95%". Yusuf, the junior analyst who pulls the data, uses the same query and cutoff date every month, so the trend stays comparable.

review: Confirm each metric you report has a goal and a target
Note any change in collection method, with the date
evidence: Saved query used to pull the data
Metric definition sheet with goal, target and owner
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the metric owner before changing a definition, and flag numbers that drive no decision.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses which metrics to track and sets their targets

subtopics.isaca_rule: A useful metric ties to a goal, has a target and changes a decision. Raw counts such as "attacks blocked" rarely do.

exam_traps.trap: More blocked attacks this month means security is improving.
exam_traps.why: Blocked counts mostly reflect how many attackers tried, not whether controls work or risk is falling.

exam_traps.trap: Switch to a better data source whenever one appears, without noting it.
exam_traps.why: A quiet method change breaks the trend. Record the change and restate the baseline.

key_terms.definition: The starting value of a measure, used to judge later change.
A number that looks impressive but does not inform a decision or show real progress.

subtopics.name: Types of Security Measures
subtopics.definition: Security measures fall into types by what they show: whether controls exist, whether they work, how fast they work and what they mean for the business.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Knowing the type stops a common mistake: reporting that a control exists as proof that it works.
how_it_works: Measurement guidance from NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) sorts measures into the four types below.
Programs usually start with implementation measures and add the others as data matures.
Mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to recover (MTTR, sometimes mean time to repair) are common efficiency measures.
Executives need impact measures; operators need implementation and efficiency measures.

types.meaning: Shows whether a control is in place, often as a percentage. Example: share of laptops with disk encryption.
Shows whether a control achieves its intended result. Example: share of simulated phishing emails that staff report.
Shows how quickly controls give feedback or problems are fixed. Example: average days to patch critical flaws.
Shows the effect on the mission or finances. Example: cost of security incidents this year.

subtopics.example: A clinic's report says "100% of staff completed phishing training". The practice manager asks whether phishing is actually being stopped. Ravi, a junior analyst, explains that completion is an implementation measure and adds two to the next report: the share of test phishing emails staff report, and the average time to report.

review: Label each reported measure by its type
Back each effectiveness claim you report with outcome data
evidence: Ticket timestamps behind detection and recovery times
Simulation data behind effectiveness figures
audit_focus.recommend: Point out to the report owner any claim of effectiveness backed only by implementation data.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides which measures appear in executive reports

subtopics.isaca_rule: Existence is not effectiveness. To show a control works, use an effectiveness measure; for executives, translate results into impact on the mission and finances.

exam_traps.trap: 100% training completion shows the awareness program is effective.
exam_traps.why: Completion is an implementation measure. Effectiveness asks whether behavior changed, such as more phishing reports.

exam_traps.trap: MTTR measures how often systems fail.
exam_traps.why: Mean time to recover is how long recovery takes on average. Failure frequency is mean time between failures (MTBF).

key_terms.definition: A metric that signals growing risk before an incident, such as a growing backlog of unpatched systems.
A metric that records outcomes after the fact, such as the number of incidents last quarter.

subtopics.name: Key Performance and Key Risk Indicators
subtopics.definition: A key performance indicator (KPI) shows how well a process meets its goal; a key risk indicator (KRI) gives early warning that a risk is growing toward its limit.
subtopics.why_it_matters: KPIs show whether security work is on track; KRIs show whether exposure is growing before it becomes an incident. Mixing them up hides warnings.
how_it_works: KPIs look at performance, such as the share of patches applied on time.
KRIs look at exposure, such as internet-facing systems with critical flaws.
Good KRIs are leading, measurable and tied to a named risk, with thresholds set from its tolerance.
The same number can be either; what matters is whether it judges performance or warns of risk.

rows.label: Example
cells: 95% of critical patches applied within 14 days
Critical flaws open more than 30 days on internet-facing servers

subtopics.example: A logistics company's quarterly supplier account review, a KPI, has been green all year. Chen, a junior analyst, notices another number climbing: supplier accounts with administrator rights and no sign-in for 90 days. He proposes it as a KRI for misused supplier access and sends the trend to the risk owner.

review: Tie each KRI you report to a named risk in the register
Compare this period's KRI values with the last
evidence: KRI history with dates, values and thresholds
Source system report behind each KRI value
audit_focus.recommend: Send worsening KRI trends to the risk owner with the source data, even before any threshold is crossed.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner decides how to respond to a worsening KRI

subtopics.isaca_rule: KPIs show performance; KRIs warn of risk. For early warning, track a leading KRI tied to a named risk, not a count of past incidents. A green KPI does not mean the risk is controlled.

exam_traps.trap: Last quarter's incident count is a good early-warning KRI.
exam_traps.why: Incident counts are lagging: they record harm already done. Early-warning KRIs track conditions that come before incidents.

exam_traps.trap: If every KPI is green, risk is under control.
exam_traps.why: A process can perform well while exposure grows elsewhere, which is why KRIs are tracked separately.

key_terms.definition: How open an asset or process is to a threat, such as an unpatched system facing the internet.
An account with administrator-level rights that could do serious harm if misused.

subtopics.name: Thresholds, Targets and Escalation
subtopics.definition: Thresholds are preset values on a metric that trigger set actions, such as review or escalation, when crossed; targets are the values the organization aims for.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A metric without a threshold relies on someone noticing a problem. Agreed thresholds make escalation automatic, so bad news reaches the right person on time.
how_it_works: Thresholds come from the risk appetite and tolerance leaders agreed.
Color bands show how close a metric is to its limit; each band names an action and an owner.
Escalation rules say how fast to report and to whom, even when the news is awkward.
Thresholds are reviewed when the appetite, the business or the threats change.

types.meaning: Within tolerance; keep monitoring as usual.
Approaching the limit; the owner named for that band reviews it and plans action.
Beyond tolerance; escalate at once by the set path, so the risk owner can act and senior management can treat or formally accept the risk.

subtopics.example: A school district's key risk indicator (KRI) for laptops missing security updates is green under 3%, amber from 3 to 8% and red above 8%. After an update tool fails, it hits 11% the week before exams. Raj, the IT technician who runs the weekly report, follows the red-band rule and alerts the IT director that afternoon.

review: Compare each new value with its threshold bands
Apply a threshold change only after its approval is recorded
evidence: Threshold table with bands, owners and actions
Escalation tickets showing when they were sent
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate breaches to the named owner as the rule requires, and never change a threshold without its owner's recorded approval.
audit_focus.decides: The named threshold owner approves changes, within tolerances senior management set

subtopics.isaca_rule: Thresholds turn numbers into action. When a metric crosses one, escalate at once; never sit on bad news, move the threshold or adjust the number.

exam_traps.trap: Raise the threshold after a breach so the KRI goes back to green.
exam_traps.why: Moving the line hides the risk without reducing it. Only the threshold's named owner changes it, with a recorded reason.

exam_traps.trap: Wait for the next scheduled report before escalating a red KRI.
exam_traps.why: Escalation rules exist so serious changes reach decision makers quickly, not at the next routine meeting.

key_terms.definition: A preset value on a metric that, once crossed, triggers a defined action.
Passing an issue to a higher authority or the right owner, using a set path and timing.

subtopics.name: Dashboards, Scorecards and Reports
subtopics.definition: Dashboards, scorecards and reports are ways to present metrics: a live visual view, a periodic grade against targets and a written account with context and recommendations.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The right numbers in the wrong format still fail. A board needs a short view of risk and trends; an operations team needs live detail.
how_it_works: Know the audience first: the board, senior management, risk owners or technical teams.
Dashboards suit people who act daily; they refresh often and allow drill-down.
Scorecards suit periodic reviews against targets; reports explain trends, causes and the decisions needed.
Show trends, not single snapshots, and use the same definitions in every view.

rows.label: Best for
cells: Operations teams watching day to day
Leaders making decisions or providing oversight

subtopics.example: A hospital's security team shows the board a 40-chart operations dashboard every quarter, and board members lose interest. The security manager replaces it with a one-page scorecard of six metrics and a short report on two risks needing a decision. Ivo, a junior analyst, writes one plain sentence under each red item on what it means for patient care.

review: Confirm the same metric shows the same value in every view
Match the level of detail to what each audience needs
evidence: Metric definition sheet used for all three formats
Board feedback on past reports
audit_focus.recommend: Flag numbers that differ between the dashboard and the report to the reporting owner before release.
audit_focus.decides: The security leader decides what is reported to the board

subtopics.isaca_rule: Fit the format to the audience and the decision. Boards get short, business-focused scorecards and reports; operations teams get live dashboards.

exam_traps.trap: Give the board the full technical dashboard so nothing is hidden.
exam_traps.why: Too much detail buries what needs board attention. Boards need summarized risk, trends and clear decisions.

exam_traps.trap: A dashboard that is all green means there is nothing to report.
exam_traps.why: Green covers only what is measured. Reports still need new risks, unmeasured areas and trends heading toward a limit.

key_terms.definition: A scorecard that tracks goals from several viewpoints, such as financial, customer and process, not just one.
Opening a dashboard figure to see the detailed data behind it.

subtopics.name: Using Measurement to Improve
subtopics.definition: Using measurement to improve means acting on what metrics show: finding causes, fixing them, checking the result and refining the metrics themselves over time.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Measuring without acting just documents decline. Metrics earn their cost only when they drive fixes and prove the fixes worked.
how_it_works: Look at trends, not one month alone, and ask why a number moved before acting.
Give each fix an owner and a due date, then measure again to confirm it worked.
Watch for gaming: once a number is a target, people may improve the number, not the outcome.
Retire metrics no one uses, and add ones for new risks such as artificial intelligence (AI) use.
subtopics.example: A software company's rate for closing vulnerability tickets within 30 days jumps from 60% to 98% in a month. Mei, a junior analyst, samples ten closed tickets and finds six marked accepted risk without the risk owner's approval. She sends the sample to the security manager, who limits that kind of closure to risk owners.

review: Check a few source records behind any sudden jump or drop
Compare the next period's figure with the pre-fix value
evidence: Source records checked against the reported figure
Action log with owners, due dates and status
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected metric gaming or poor data quality to the security manager with the records you checked.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides improvement priorities and funds the actions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat a sudden improvement with the same curiosity as a sudden drop. Check the data behind a metric before trusting it; gaming a metric is a governance problem to report.

exam_traps.trap: A metric that hits its target proves the risk is handled.
exam_traps.why: Targets can be met by gaming or by measuring the wrong thing. Check that the outcome behind the number improved.

exam_traps.trap: Keep every metric forever so the history is complete.
exam_traps.why: Unused metrics waste effort and clutter reports. Retire them on purpose, keeping their history.

key_terms.definition: Changing behavior to improve a number without improving the result it is meant to show.
The underlying reason a problem happened, which a fix must address to stop it recurring.

subtopics.name: AI Risk Indicators
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) risk indicators are metrics that warn when an AI system's accuracy, data, use or availability is moving toward unacceptable risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI systems can fail quietly: accuracy slips or staff turn to unapproved tools. AI key risk indicators (KRIs) give owners time to act before a service is disrupted.
how_it_works: Accuracy against a held-back test set, tracked over time, signals model drift.
A growing human override rate, meaning staff reject the AI's output more often, suggests declining quality.
Use of unapproved AI tools shows policy risk; AI service outages, including at providers, show continuity risk.
Each AI KRI has an owner, thresholds and an escalation path, like any other KRI.
subtopics.example: A theme park plans an AI assistant that answers visitors' questions about tickets and opening hours. Before launch, the model owner asks Ade, a junior analyst, to help set its key risk indicators. Ade proposes tracking the share of a weekly sample of answers that cite a made-up price or park rule, often called hallucinations: amber at 2% alerts the model owner, and red at 5% also goes to the risk owner.

review: Tie each AI KRI you report to a model in the AI inventory
Report threshold crossings to the model owner with the trend
evidence: Dashboard history of accuracy and override rates
Web proxy blocks for unapproved AI sites
audit_focus.recommend: Report AI KRI breaches to the model owner and the risk owner as the escalation path requires.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides whether to retrain, roll back or pause

subtopics.isaca_rule: Measure AI like any critical risk: leading indicators, an owner, thresholds and escalation. A model can look healthy on uptime while drifting on accuracy, so track both.

exam_traps.trap: AI service uptime of 99.9% shows the AI risk is low.
exam_traps.why: Uptime shows the service answers, not that its answers are right.

exam_traps.trap: AI risk indicators are only for data scientists.
exam_traps.why: AI KRIs belong in the same dashboards and reports as other risks, where leaders can see them.

key_terms.definition: A change in the input data an AI system receives compared with the data it learned from.
How often people reject or change an AI system's output; a growing rate can signal declining quality.

key_terminologies.Governance, risk and compliance (GRC): A joined-up way of directing an organization, managing its risks and meeting its obligations.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: The amount and type of risk leaders are willing to take to pursue their goals.
key_terminologies.Data owner: The business leader accountable for a data set, who decides its classification and who may access it.
key_terminologies.Custodian: The person or team, often IT, that looks after data or systems as the owner directs.
key_terminologies.RACI chart: A table showing, for each task, who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed.
key_terminologies.Framework: A published structure of practices or controls that organizes security work, such as the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Cybersecurity Framework.
key_terminologies.Compliance: Meeting the laws, regulations, contracts and internal policies that apply, and being able to prove it.
key_terminologies.Redundancy: Spare components or paths that take over when one fails.
key_terminologies.High availability (HA): Keeping a service running with very little downtime, using redundancy and failover.
key_terminologies.Business continuity (BC): Keeping critical business functions running during and after a disruption.
key_terminologies.Disaster recovery (DR): Restoring the technology and data that business functions depend on.
key_terminologies.Business impact analysis (BIA): A study of critical functions, their dependencies and how harm grows over time when they stop.
key_terminologies.Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD): The longest a function can be down before harm becomes unacceptable.
key_terminologies.Recovery time objective (RTO): The target time to restore a function; it must fit within the MTD.
key_terminologies.Recovery point objective (RPO): The most data, measured in time, the business can afford to lose.
key_terminologies.Hot site: A recovery site with equipment, connections and current data, ready within minutes to hours.
key_terminologies.Cold site: A recovery site with space, power and cooling only; equipping it takes days to weeks.
key_terminologies.Immutable backup: A backup that cannot be changed or deleted until its retention period ends.
key_terminologies.Model drift: A gradual decline in an AI model's accuracy as real-world conditions change.
key_terminologies.Security culture: The shared attitudes and habits that shape how people treat security every day.
key_terminologies.Social engineering: Manipulating people, instead of systems, to gain information, access or money.
key_terminologies.Phishing: A fake message that pretends to come from a trusted source to trick the reader.
key_terminologies.Deepfake: AI-generated or AI-altered audio or video that imitates a real person.
key_terminologies.Passphrase: A long password made of several words, easier to remember and hard to guess.
key_terminologies.Multifactor authentication (MFA): Signing in with two or more different kinds of proof.
key_terminologies.Metric: A measure compared with a goal or target to show progress or risk.
key_terminologies.Key performance indicator (KPI): A metric showing how well a process meets its goal.
key_terminologies.Key risk indicator (KRI): A metric giving early warning that a risk is growing toward its limit.
key_terminologies.Dashboard: A visual, frequently updated view of metrics for people who act on them daily.
key_terminologies.Scorecard: A periodic summary of results against targets, often color-coded.
